ch03.card: Part 2 of 10. The reader: giving every letter a meaning.
ch03.s01.c1: Who reads your question first? A model called Gemma, and we did not build it. We borrowed it, and it reads the whole question one time.
ch03.s01.c2: Picture a translator who already knows English well. That is a picture only. We cannot change him. Hold on to that.
ch03.s02.c1: How would you cut up a sentence? Gemma cuts text into word pieces, called tokens. These cuts in Tom has 12 apples are a made-up example, a picture only.
ch03.s02.c2: Our thinker, the part that does the thinking, works on letters. It has one spot for each letter, not each word piece.
ch03.s03.c1: Guess: how many letters does one piece cover? On 20,000 of our skill questions, 3.08 letters on average. We measured that by count.
ch03.s03.c2: On 9,068 web-text chunks of 279 letters, 4.27 letters per token on average.
ch03.s04.c1: Gemma reads the whole question one time, then never looks again.
ch03.s04.c2: Each token gets a note card of 768 numbers, its meaning in context.
ch03.s04.c3: Each letter takes the card of the token it sits in, so they share its meaning.
ch03.s05.c1: How much does it hold? 271,002,624 numbers, all set before our work began.
ch03.s05.c2: About 134 million are a word table, one row per word piece. About 137 million are reading layers, plus a step widening rows to 768.
ch03.s05.c3: And it is frozen. Our practice never changes it. Its reading limit is 8,192 tokens, which is not our limit.
ch03.s06.c1: In the small test models, a converter plug, one learned layer, turns Gemma's 768 numbers into the thinker's width.
ch03.s06.c2: At width 256 it has about 197 thousand learned numbers. At full size there is no plug: Gemma's 512 numbers go straight in.
ch03.s07.c1: Now each letter gets a recipe. First: which letter it is. A learned row of numbers.
ch03.s07.c2: Second: where it sits in the question. A learned table: 2,000 rows in the planned finished design, B3, and 280 in the growth test, G1.
ch03.s07.c3: Third: how far its letter sits from the end of its word. The count is hand-written, but the row it picks is learned.
ch03.s07.c4: Fourth: Gemma's meaning is added on top, by a small plug, none at full size. The window reads the sum.
ch03.s08.c1: Two small learned layers read the summed row. They are ours, not borrowed.
ch03.s08.c2: Each layer looks 2 letters left and 2 right, so a letter sees 4 letters each side. It peeks at its neighbours.
ch03.s08.c3: The window adds about 0.7 million numbers at width 256, about 2.6 million at 512. Remember it.
ch03.s09.c1: Now take the window away. Guess the score. Cipher puzzles are one kind of test question: 40 familiar-style ones per copy, a separate training run, scored out of 100.
ch03.s09.c2: With the window, Gemma plus letters scores 97.5 and 95.0 on two copies.
ch03.s09.c3: Without it, Gemma plus letters scores 5.0 and 2.5.
ch03.s09.c4: Letters alone, without it, score 12.5 and 2.5. Tested on only two copies, one kind of question.
ch03.s10.c1: The position table has one row per spot, so it sets the longest question: 280 letters in the growth test, G1, and 2,000 in planned B3.
ch03.s10.c2: How many questions run too long? In a sample of 4,000 bAbI test questions, a public set of story puzzles, 32% run over 280 letters and 1% over 2,000.
ch03.s11.c1: Built versions: a hand pattern finds numbers. The new design copies none.
ch03.s11.c2: It records where each number is, not its value.
ch03.s11.c3: Room to mark: 16 numbers in the calculator-outside model, T1SDR, 91 in the growth test, G1, 240 in planned B3.
ch03.s12.c1: New design: each calculator reply, sub 12, 5 equals 7, is read by Gemma plus the letter window.
ch03.s12.c2: The built B3 version: the window alone reads replies.
ch03.s12.c3: Never tested. The old reason, that Gemma adds nothing to a reply, was only suggested.
ch03.s13.c1: Did borrowing a reader help? On 6,040 test questions kept aside, five kinds called Pooled-5, six separate training runs, or copies, with the reader scored 75.9 to 77.2.
ch03.s13.c2: Eight copies of the same model without the reader scored 73.0 to 74.7.
ch03.s13.c3: On average the reader is ahead by 2.67 points out of 100, in all 6 copies, at 3M, about 3 million learned numbers.
ch03.s14.c1: But there is a catch. A leak means answers right with zero rounds of thinking.
ch03.s14.c2: We set a warning light in advance. Averaged over 6 copies, the zero-round leak is 6.59. The pass mark, no-reader average plus 1.0, was 4.62. Missed.
ch03.s14.c3: On seed 200, on familiar questions, the reader version scored 18.09 with zero rounds. The same model without it scored 1.40.
ch03.s14.c4: Copies without the reader leak on some seeds too, so the cause is not settled.
ch03.s15.c1: A test called TK would give the thinker one spot per token, or word piece, instead of one per letter.
ch03.s15.c2: The code and a PC job file exist, but it has never been run, so there is no result. Letters or tokens is undecided.
ch03.s16.c1: The reader is borrowed and frozen. It reads once.
ch03.s16.c2: Each letter gets a meaning in context, plus a window of 4 letters each side.
ch03.s16.c3: Without the window, the Gemma version scored 5.0 and 2.5 out of 100 on cipher puzzles, in two copies. So where does the thinking happen? Next: the thinker.
